newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's unemployment drops sharply in March.
newsitem.headline: Canada's unemployment drops sharply in March.

text.p: Canada's job market finally showed signs of life on Friday when the national statistics agency said that the country's unemployment rate fell to 9.3 percent in March, its lowest point in 18 months.
The drop exceeded expectations and was a sharp improvement from the 9.7 percent rate at which unemployment was stuck in recent months.
Canada saw the creation of 60,900 jobs in March, increasing employment to 13.8 million, Statistics Canada said. Employment had fallen by 18,700 jobs in February.

The job growth could increase the likelihood of a federal election this spring and prompted speculation that the Bank of Canada might raise interest rates soon, reversing a long trend of steady rate reductions.

"It's certainly good news for the Canadian economy," said economist Sherry Cooper at brokerage Nesbitt Burns in Toronto. "I believe any tightening by the Bank (of Canada) would really just be a confirmation of what has already happened in the markets."
Although the Bank of Canada made no move to raise key interest rates on Friday, Cooper said she was certain a rate hike was in the cards in the near future.
"Clearly what we have seen here is that the Canadian economy is indeed performing very well and it doesn't need any further stimulus," said economist Michael Gregory at Lehman Brothers in Toronto.
But the governing Liberals' enthusiasm about the labor numbers was muted.

"I think it's better that the unemployment rate went down, rather than go up," Industry Minister John Manley told reporters. "But there's still a major problem with the number of unemployed Canadians. I don't think anyone should take too much comfort in a few percentage points decline in the unemployment rate. It'a big challenge for us."

Showing a streak of independence from the U.S. Federal Reserve, Canada has held its interest rates steady despite a recent U.S. rate hike -- a move that sent the Canadian dollar sliding to C$1.3926 (71.81 U.S. cents) on Thursday -- its lowest level in two years against the U.S. currency.
The Canadian dollar strengthened slightly on Friday after the labor report to C$1.3899 (71.94 U.S. cents).
